title: Research methods and statistics

read.title: Why random assignment matters
text: Suppose researchers notice that students who drink coffee get higher grades. Does coffee improve learning? A correlation like this cannot answer the question. Coffee drinkers might also sleep less, study more, or come from different backgrounds. Any of these third variables could produce the link, and it is even possible that working hard leads students to drink coffee rather than the reverse.

To test cause and effect, researchers run an experiment. They decide what to manipulate, the independent variable, such as caffeine or no caffeine. They decide what to measure, the dependent variable, such as a quiz score, and give it an operational definition so others can repeat the study.

The key step is random assignment. Each participant has an equal chance of landing in the experimental or control group, so differences in sleep, motivation or background tend to balance out across groups. If the groups then differ on the quiz, the manipulation is the most likely cause.

A double-blind design adds protection: neither participants nor researchers know who got caffeine, so expectations cannot quietly shape the results. Finally, a statistical test asks whether the difference is larger than chance alone would usually produce.
